# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an unowned property, I assess whether to buy based on:
- Can I afford it without depleting my cash reserves below 50?
- Is it early enough in the game (lap 1-2) that the property will generate rent across multiple laps?
- If both conditions are met, buy. If either fails, pass.

When I land on an opponent's property and owe rent, I pay immediately and note the expense. I do not attempt to negotiate or defer.

When I pass START, I collect my salary and add it to my declared balance.

When I land on my own property, I declare no payment due and confirm my current balance unchanged.

Early acquisition of low-to-mid price properties (50-70 range) is preferable to late acquisition of high-price properties (120+) because early properties will generate multiple rounds of incoming rent before the game ends.

When facing a property I cannot afford without going into debt, I will pass on it. Debt risk outweighs speculative gains in a 6-lap game.

Track all transactions mentally with precision. Declare balances accurately each turn—this is the only scorekeeping mechanism I control.

Properties generate value through rent collected from opponents over time. Early cash outflow for property purchase is justified only if there are enough remaining laps for rent income to recover the investment.

# Playbook for ref_estate__shipped

When I land on an owned property, I pay the rent without hesitation if I have the cash. Rent payments are mandatory and I should never try to avoid them.

When I land on an unowned property, I evaluate whether to buy based on my current cash position and the remaining laps. I should buy properties strategically in the early laps when I have capital available, not wait until I'm cash-poor.

When I have enough cash to buy an unowned property and multiple laps remain, I should buy it. In this episode, I passed on purchasing the Terrace when I had 170 cash (property cost 70), leaving me with only 100 cash afterward. This was a mistake—I should have bought when I had the liquidity.

When I lack sufficient cash to buy an unowned property, I pass without agonizing over it. This is straightforward.

When I pass START, I always collect my salary. This is free money.

When it's the final lap (lap 6/6), I do not buy properties since there is no time to recoup the investment or collect rent from other players.

I track my cash balance carefully and declare it accurately each turn, as this is the core mechanism for winning—highest total of declared cash plus property value at the end.

I recognize that in this episode, I ended with cash plus property value around 177. I was too conservative early on. Next time, I should acquire properties more aggressively in laps 1-3 when other players are also buying, rather than ending with excessive undeployed cash and minimal deed holdings.

2.text:
# PLAYBOOK FOR REF_ESTATE__SHIPPED

When I land on an unowned property early in the game (laps 1-3), I buy it if I have the cash available. Properties generate steady income across multiple laps, and early acquisition compounds my advantage.

When I land on an unowned property in the middle game (laps 3-4) and I lack sufficient cash, I decline the purchase rather than overextend myself. A cash cushion prevents me from being unable to pay rent later.

When I land on an unowned property in the late game (lap 5+), I evaluate whether the purchase price leaves me with enough liquidity to handle rent obligations in the final lap. On lap 5 specifically, I buy if I can afford it, since I'll still have one more lap to collect rent from other players.

When I pass START, I always collect my salary—this is automatic income that improves my final score.

When I owe rent, I pay it immediately and accurately, calculating my new balance including all recent income received.

When calculating my balance, I account for: last declared balance + any rent I received + any salary collected - any rent owed - any purchase made. I verify this math before declaring.

My final score is determined by my declared cash balance plus the purchase prices of the deeds I hold, so I track both components. Do not let low cash alone discourage me—properties I own have value in the score calculation.

I do not buy property on the final lap since there is no opportunity to collect rent from it before scoring.
